article.title: How to Say I Miss You in Arabic to a Woman
article.excerpt: To a woman it is اشتقت إليكِ; to a man, اشتقت إليكَ. The kasra that separates them appears in 2 of 51 attested sentences, so the feminine form usually arrives looking identical to the masculine. Egyptian marks her with a letter instead.
article.metaTitle: How to Say I Miss You in Arabic to a Woman — One Silent Mark
article.metaDescription: I miss you in Arabic to a woman is اشتقت إليكِ, but the kasra that marks her is written in only 2 of 51 attested sentences. Egyptian uses a full letter.

keyTakeaways: To a woman the Modern Standard form is اشتقت إليكِ (ishtaqtu ilayki); the only difference from the masculine اشتقت إليكَ is a kasra, and 46 of 51 attested Tatoeba sentences write no mark at all.
Egyptian وحشتيني marks her with a full letter, ي, so the feminine survives being typed; the Modern Standard form does not.
مشتاقة marks the gender of the person writing, not the person addressed — two of the nine ranking results get this backwards.
Wiktionary's "I miss you" phrasebook lists 69 languages and exactly two entries carry gender tags; both are Arabic.
Across 214 pages on SubhSandesh's miss-you template, 92.1% carry an "open when" letter and 13.6% a voice note — the only channel measured in which the vowel can actually be heard.

faqs.question: Is اشتقت إليكِ right for a girlfriend as well as a wife?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic marks the addressee's gender, not the relationship, so the same form covers a girlfriend, a wife, a sister and a friend. Wiktionary's phrasebook gives one feminine entry, أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكِ, with no relationship qualifier attached to it.

faqs.question: Will she actually see the difference if I type it on my phone?
faqs.answer: Usually not. The kasra is a nonspacing mark and running Arabic leaves it off — in the Tatoeba corpus, 2 of 51 sentences containing إليك write it and 46 write neither mark. If you want the difference to be visible, use the Egyptian form, where it is a full letter, or write it in Latin letters.

faqs.question: Does it change if I am a woman writing to another woman?
faqs.answer: Not in اشتقت إليكِ. The verb form اشتقت is first person and carries no gender for the speaker, so only her gender is marked. It does change if you use the participle: مشتاقة marks you as the woman writing, and you would still need لكِ for her.

faqs.question: Is أشتاق إليكِ different from اشتقت إليكِ?
faqs.answer: They are the present and the past of the same form-VIII verb on root ش و ق. Wiktionary's phrasebook prints the present, أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكِ, as the headline translation; Tatoeba attests both, with seven sentences using the past اشتقت إليك all translated "I miss you".

faqs.question: What do I send if I do not know which dialect she speaks?
faqs.answer: The Modern Standard pair is the one every reader of Arabic will parse, and it is the only entry Wiktionary's phrasebook gives for Arabic as a whole. Egyptian وحشتيني is the widest-travelled dialect form, but it is regional, and no reference instrument I could reach carries a Levantine or Gulf version at all.

faqs.question: Can I just write it in English letters instead?
faqs.answer: That is Arabizi, and for this sentence it is more precise than the Arabic script, because the final vowel becomes a full Latin character: ishta2t elayki cannot be confused with ishta2t elayka. Bies and colleagues built an entire ACL corpus around how routinely Arabic speakers do this in SMS and chat.

faqs.question: Why do dictionaries show four different spellings of the same phrase?
faqs.answer: Because the vocalisation is optional, so each vowelled variant gets indexed separately. Glosbe carries اِشْتَقْتُ لَك, اِشْتَقْتُ لِك, اَشْتَقْتُ لَكِ and the bare اشتقت لك as four headwords, all glossed "I miss you", and evidences all four with the same single unvocalised sentence.

faqs.question: What about افتقدتك — is that the same thing?
faqs.answer: It is a different root. Wiktionary glosses افتقد as "to miss; to lose", and also "to examine; to study". It reads cooler and more written than اشتقت, and it takes the same gendered ending, so the same problem applies to it.

faqs.question: Does the hub page on saying I miss you in different languages cover this?
faqs.answer: Only partly. It gives Arabic a single line, أشتاق إليك, with two transliterations, ash-taaq ilayk and ash-taaq ilayki. The gender distinction is there in the romanisation but not in the Arabic script it prints, which is exactly the gap this page exists to fill.

faqs.question: Should I put the transliteration under the Arabic when I send it?
faqs.answer: If she reads Arabic, no — it reads like a language lesson. If you are writing on a page whose layout is English and left-to-right, a line of Arabic with nothing around it can look accidental, and one line of romanisation underneath is what stops it looking that way.

article.contentMarkdown:
# How to Say I Miss You in Arabic to a Woman

To say I miss you in Arabic to a woman, write **اشتقت إليكِ** (*ishtaqtu ilayki*); to a man the same sentence is **اشتقت إليكَ** (*ishtaqtu ilayka*). The only difference is the final mark, a kasra, U+0650 — and everyday Arabic leaves it off. Of the 51 sentences in the Tatoeba corpus containing إليك, two write it. So the feminine form the search results hand you usually reaches her phone looking identical to the masculine one. Egyptian differs: **وحشتيني** marks her with a full letter, ي, which no keyboard strips. On SubhSandesh's own miss-you pages the median gap between first save and last edit is 2.6 hours (n=214), and 88.8% of started pages get published and shared (190 of 214) — this is a line senders go back and change.

## Arabic has three feminines here, and they are not in the same word

There is no single "feminine form" of this sentence. There are three slots where a woman's gender can be marked, and which one you land in decides whether she ever sees it.

In Modern Standard Arabic it sits on the **object pronoun** — the kasra under the last letter of إليكِ. In Egyptian it sits on the **verb's subject ending**, because وحش inverts the sentence and makes her the one acting on you, so the mark is the ي inside وحشتيني. In the participle مشتاق it sits on **the speaker**, not on her at all.

That this is an Arabic problem and not a general one is checkable. [Wiktionary's "I miss you" phrasebook](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/I_miss_you) lists 69 languages, and exactly two entries carry masculine and feminine tags — both Arabic: أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكَ `m` and أَشْتَاقُ إِلَيْكِ `f`, then Egyptian وحشتني `m` (*waḥašteni*) and وحشتيني `f` (*waḥaštīni*).

## The mark that 49 of 51 attested sentences leave out

The masculine ending is U+0643 U+064E, kaf plus fatha; the feminine U+0643 U+0650, kaf plus kasra. Both marks are nonspacing, so the string is the same width with or without them — and they are usually without. Searching [the Tatoeba corpus](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/392778) for إليك returns 52 Arabic sentences, 51 of them containing the pronoun: three write the masculine fatha, two the feminine kasra, and 46 neither.

Neither feminine-marked sentence is about missing anyone: one is أحتاج إليكِ, "I need you", the other a translated speech addressing أمريكا, a feminine noun. And of the seven sentences containing اشتقت إليك, all translated "I miss you", not one carries either mark.

## مشتاقة is the feminine of "I", not the feminine of "you"

Here two page-one results go wrong in a way you can check in a dictionary. [Wiktionary files مُشْتَاق](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%85%D8%B4%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%82) as the active participle of اِشْتَاقَ, declined as an adjective and glossed "yearning (for), longing (for), desirous".

An adjective agrees with whoever it describes, and that is the person doing the longing. Tatoeba bears it out: أنا مشتاق لك is "I miss you" with a masculine speaker, and زوجها مشتاق لها is "Her husband is missing her". The ة is about the writer.

Two of the nine results print it the other way round — welcome2jordan says "Mishtaq (مشتاق) is used when speaking to a man, mishtaqa (مشتاقه) when speaking to a woman", and equranzone answers "what do you say to a woman?" with مشتاقة لك. A man who copies that sends a sentence with both gender marks on the wrong people: feminine on himself, unmarked on her.

## One result offers "I love you" and one offers "I forget you"

The sixth result, wordscr, lists بحبك as "I miss you in a loving way" and بحبك كتير as "I miss you a lot". [Wiktionary's Egyptian Arabic entry for بحبك](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%A8%D8%AD%D8%A8%D9%83) carries exactly one gloss: **I love you**. It is built on ح ب ب, love, not ش و ق or و ح ش.

The same page gives Egyptian بنسىك, transcribed "b-nes-ik", for "I miss you". That is the imperfect of نسي, which Wiktionary's Egyptian Arabic entry defines as "to forget (to lose remembrance of)". Send it and you have told her you forget her.

## What the nine ranking pages actually give you

Measured on 2026-09-25 against the India-served result set. Two of the nine — both howtosayguide.com URLs, at positions 1 and 4 — timed out on every attempt, so these counts are out of the seven that returned.

Six of seven give a feminine form; wordscr gives none. Five of seven write the kasra on the feminine. Exactly one, alifbee, also writes the fatha on the masculine — so six of seven treat the feminine as the marked special case and the masculine as the plain default, which is not how the two sit in the grammar. Six of seven name a dialect; sahraiq names none while presenting the dialectal لـ construction as simply "Arabic". Zero of seven mention Arabizi, which is how most of this gets typed.

## Five ways to write it, and whose gender each one carries

The last column names the field on a miss-you page where each form tends to land. The percentages are measured; the assignment is my judgement, not something the database records.

| What you send | Whose gender it marks | How the feminine is marked | Survives plain typing? | Where it sits on a miss-you page (n=214) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| اشتقت إليكِ | the woman you are writing to | kasra, a nonspacing mark | No — 2 of 51 attested sentences keep it | The letter, median 88 words |
| وحشتيني | the woman you are writing to | ي, a full letter | Yes | The letter, median 88 words |
| اِشْتَقْتُ لِك | the woman you are writing to | kasra on the ل | No | One of the 3.2 "open when" letters per page |
| مشتاقة لكِ | the woman writing | ة on the participle | Yes — but it marks you, not her | 13.6% record a voice note (29 of 214) |
| ishta2t elayki | the woman you are writing to | a Latin *i* | Yes | The 4.5 written memories per page |

## Arabizi is the only typed form that keeps her gender

[Arabizi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabizi) is Arabic written in Latin letters, with digits for the sounds Latin has no letter for — 7 for ح, 3 for ع. Because the final vowel becomes a full character rather than a mark, *ishta2t elayki* is unmissably different from *ishta2t elayka*.

This is not fringe. [Bies and colleagues, at the 2014 ACL workshop on Arabic NLP](https://aclanthology.org/W14-3612/), built a parallel Arabizi–Arabic script SMS and chat corpus because "Arabic speakers in social media as well as discussion forums, SMS messaging and online chat often use a non-standard romanization called Arabizi", and because the dialects used there "lack standard orthographies".

The reading research points the same way. In a PRISMA review of studies from 2000 to 2025, [Asadi and Asli-Badarneh](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13050341) argue that diglossia and the visual complexity of the script are "multiplicative but not additive" challenges, ending on the need to scaffold readers "as they transition from vowelized to unvowelized text". Abstract only; the full text was not readable.

## Which Arabic you are writing, and what it is actually called

Six codes, checked against the ISO 639-3 registry on 2026-09-25, all Active, individual, living members of the macrolanguage Arabic: `arb` Standard Arabic, `arz` Egyptian, `apc` Levantine, `acm` Mesopotamian — the registry's name for what everyone calls Iraqi — `afb` Gulf, `ary` Moroccan.

Now the awkward part. The phrasebook covers `ar` and `arz` and nothing else. Tatoeba returns zero sentences for اشتقتلك and zero for وحشتيني, and [Glosbe](https://glosbe.com/ar/en/%D8%A7%D9%90%D8%B4%D8%AA%D9%8E%D9%82%D9%92%D8%AA%D9%8F%20%D9%84%D9%90%D9%83) has no entry for اشتقتلك either. So the Levantine, Gulf and Maghrebi feminine forms the ranking pages print confidently are not in any reference instrument I could reach, and I am not printing them.

What Glosbe does carry is the لـ construction, under four separately vocalised headwords — اِشْتَقْتُ لَك, اِشْتَقْتُ لِك, اَشْتَقْتُ لَكِ and the bare اشتقت لك — each glossed "I miss you", and each evidenced by the same single example sentence, itself written without any of those marks. The dictionary distinguishes four forms, then proves all four with one piece of text that cannot tell them apart.

## Where the line goes, and where our own page loses

The sentence is two words; what carries it is whatever you wrap around it, and that part is measurable. 92.1% of miss-you pages carry an "open when" letter (197 of 214), 86.4% a written memory (185 of 214), and 47 distinct city pairs appear across them, including Mumbai–London.

The [miss-you page for a partner](/missyou-gf) is the honest home for this, with one real limitation: its headings, buttons and layout are English and left-to-right, so an Arabic line sits inside furniture running the other way. If the whole message is Arabic, a letter in her language with the page as a frame reads better than one line stranded in English chrome.

Three caveats travel with those numbers. The city, background-music and "together since" fields are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates are not sender choices. `viewCount` counts page views, not unique visitors. And n=214 over two months since 2026-07-28, so nothing seasonal survives it. One more disclosure: the database records which template was opened, never who received it, so none of this describes the women these pages went to.

If the missing is about time rather than distance, [the Capsule page](/capsule) — you both write predictions and open them together later — fits better, because it gives the waiting a shape. If neither suits, [the full template list](/templates) is the place to look.

## What this page is not

It is not the general Arabic answer. [I Miss You in Arabic](/blog/i-miss-you-in-arabic) covers which verb to use and why وحشتني inverts the sentence; this page covers only the addressee's gender — where it is marked, and whether it survives typing. It is also the depth under the hub on [saying I miss you in different languages](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages), which gives Arabic one line, أشتاق إليك, with two transliterations, *ash-taaq ilayk* and *ash-taaq ilayki*. Even there the distinction lives in the romanisation, not the script beside it.

## Sources

- [Wiktionary, "I miss you" phrasebook](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/I_miss_you) — 69 languages; only Arabic and Egyptian Arabic carry gender tags.
- [Wiktionary, مشتاق](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D9%85%D8%B4%D8%AA%D8%A7%D9%82) — active participle of اِشْتَاقَ, declined as an adjective.
- [Wiktionary, بحبك](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%A8%D8%AD%D8%A8%D9%83) — Egyptian Arabic phrase, "I love you".
- [Tatoeba, Arabic sentences](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/392778) — CC BY 2.0 FR.
- [Glosbe, اِشْتَقْتُ لِك](https://glosbe.com/ar/en/%D8%A7%D9%90%D8%B4%D8%AA%D9%8E%D9%82%D9%92%D8%AA%D9%8F%20%D9%84%D9%90%D9%83) — dictionary headword.
- [Asadi and Asli-Badarneh, "Diglossia and Orthographic Complexity in Arabic"](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13050341) — *Journal of Psycholinguistic Research* 55, 2026. Abstract only.
- [Bies et al., "Transliteration of Arabizi into Arabic Orthography"](https://aclanthology.org/W14-3612/) — EMNLP 2014 Workshop on Arabic NLP, ACL. Abstract only.
